  unshared. There is also a deliberate theological echo in "word," the sense of a command that
  brings a world into being, which is not really an exaggeration of what a shell does: you speak,
  and files exist or cease to exist. If the haiku has a seasonal feeling, a kigo in the traditional
  sense, it is late night — the hour when the room is dark, the screen is the only light, and the
  cursor's rhythm becomes the only clock. And underneath all three lines runs the quiet joke that
  makes the form appropriate to the subject: a haiku is seventeen syllables of severe constraint
  that must nonetheless summon an entire world, which is also a fair description of a command line.

✻ Worked for 26s
